1Purpose

This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to when it assesses a participant's behaviour and writes their behaviour support plan. It is for participants, their families and advocates, the people who carry out their plans, and the people who check our work.

We treat behaviour as a way of communicating a need. Our plans aim first to improve the participant's quality of life. They aim second to reduce the need for behaviours that put anyone at risk.

2Applies to

  • Every behaviour support assessment and every behaviour support plan that [Provider name] writes, interim or comprehensive, with or without a regulated restrictive practice.
  • Every Practitioner, including a contractor, and every manager who supports their work.
  • Only a specialist behaviour support provider. A provider that only carries out plans uses POL-BSP-03 Supporting the Assessment and Development of Behaviour Support Plans Policy.

"Behaviour Support Rules" in this policy means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

We will have every assessment and every plan written by a Practitioner whom the Commissioner considers suitable, and by no one else.

4Ground rules

G1

Only a Practitioner assesses or writes a plan. Workers, family and managers give information and keep records. A manager never signs an assessment or a plan.

G2

A decision maker decides only what their legal authority covers. For a child, a person with parental responsibility decides. A family member without that authority is consulted with the participant's consent, and is never asked to consent for an adult. The law of [state or territory] says who may consent.

G3

Before we decide what a behaviour means, we ask a health practitioner to review pain, illness, medicine effects and sleep. We also look at unmet communication needs. A behaviour may be the only way the participant can say something is wrong. If the review has not happened when the report is due, the function statement is marked provisional and FRM-SBS-03 Q24 records the dated request and the date to chase it.

G4

An assessment report never recommends a restrictive practice. If one may be needed, the Practitioner starts PRO-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) before the plan is written.

G5

A Practitioner never copies another participant's plan. Every strategy rests on this participant's own assessment.

G6

We enter nothing that identifies a participant into an automated or AI tool that POL-TEC-01 Artificial Intelligence and Automated Tools Policy has not approved. A tool never writes a finding, a strategy or a plan. The Practitioner reads, decides and signs.

G7

The engagement date is the date we agree in writing to develop the plan, or the date a regulated restrictive practice was first used, whichever is earlier. Where that use was before the referral reached us, the engagement date is the date the referral reached us (our standard). The date we first do assessment or plan work counts as agreeing to develop the plan. A later date named in a service agreement never moves it. The Behaviour Support Rules do not define "engaged", so this is our standard, and it is the earliest reading.

G8

A plan is in force from the date the Practitioner finalises and signs it. We count every 12 month review from that date. A typing correction or a small update to a skill program is not a review.

G9

Our standard is to finish the assessment report within 49 days, and the comprehensive plan within 84 days, of the engagement date. The step limits in PRO-BSP-03 add up to about 77 days, inside that target. Where the law sets a time limit, nobody at [Provider name] can extend it. A Practitioner who will miss any limit tells the Service Manager at once.

G10

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. A sole Practitioner does the Service Manager and Quality Manager tasks themselves, except that the decision whether an incident is reportable is made by the outside Clinical Supervisor with them. The Clinical Supervisor is always someone outside [Provider name], named in REG-SBS-01 col K, and does the Service Manager's checks on the sole Practitioner's own work. The Clinical Supervisor also receives any concern about the sole Practitioner's own work.

G11

A plan that contains a regulated restrictive practice holds every element of the Commission's current plan checklist and the restrictive practice protocol, and the Practitioner lodges it in the Commission's portal with the information and attachments the portal requires. It may be on the Commission's template, our own approved template or the template a state or territory authorising body requires (Behaviour Support Rules, section 23(1)). We check the Commission's current checklist and template edition on the day we start a plan and never reuse a saved copy without that check.

G12

We write a plan when a behaviour affects a participant's quality of life or puts anyone at risk of harm. We do this whether or not a restrictive practice is involved.

G13

At every stage we use the participant's own way of communicating, and we respect their culture and language.

Clinical Lead: the most senior Clinical Supervisor, who owns clinical practice at [Provider name] and the policies and procedures in POL-SBS-03 to POL-SBS-07. Where there is only one Clinical Supervisor, they are the Clinical Lead. In a sole practitioner provider, the outside Clinical Supervisor is the Clinical Lead.

  • Practitioner: an NDIS behaviour support practitioner. This is a person the Commissioner considers suitable to assess behaviour and write plans that may include restrictive practices (Behaviour Support Rules, section 5). A contractor who meets this test is a Practitioner.
  • Clinical Supervisor: the person who supervises a Practitioner's work and checks each assessment report and each plan. In a sole provider this is someone outside [Provider name].
  • Clinical Lead: where we have more than one Clinical Supervisor, the most senior; otherwise the Clinical Supervisor. In a sole practitioner provider, the outside Clinical Supervisor.
  • behaviour support assessment: the wide look at a participant's life, health, needs and supports that comes before a comprehensive plan. It includes the functional behaviour assessment.
  • functional behaviour assessment: working out the function or purpose of a behaviour. We use data, observation and information about what sets it off and keeps it going. The Behaviour Support Rules call it a functional behavioural assessment.
  • assessment report: the written record of the behaviour support assessment. We write it on FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template.
  • plan: a behaviour support plan, interim or comprehensive.
  • interim plan: a plan written quickly to reduce immediate risk while the assessment is done.
  • comprehensive plan: the full plan that rests on the assessment.
  • regulated restrictive practice: seclusion, chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, physical restraint or environmental restraint, as section 6 of the Behaviour Support Rules defines them.
  • engagement date: the date we agree in writing to develop the plan, or the date a regulated restrictive practice was first used, whichever is earlier (ground rule 7).
  • support network: the family, carers, friends and advocates the participant chooses.
  • decision maker: a person with legal authority to decide for the participant, for example a guardian.
  • engagement date: the earliest of the date we agree, in any form, to develop the plan, the date we first do assessment or plan work, and the date the service agreement starts; or the date a regulated restrictive practice is first used after the referral reaches us, if that is earlier. Ground rule 7 explains it.
  • in force: a plan is in force from the date the Practitioner finalises and signs it.
  • Commissioner: the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commissioner. The Commission is the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission.

docs.html:
1Purpose

The result: every participant we assess gets an assessment that finds their unmet needs and the function of their behaviour. They get a plan written with them and with the people who carry it out. Those providers accept it, and a plan with a regulated restrictive practice reaches the Commissioner on time.

This procedure gives effect to POL-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessments and Behaviour Support Plans Policy, C1 to C14.

"Behaviour Support Rules" means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

2When and who

Start this procedure when:

  • we receive a referral for a behaviour support assessment or plan
  • we take over a participant from another specialist provider
  • a review under PRO-SBS-04 Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure says a plan must change, or the assessment revisit date is within 30 days.

Only a specialist behaviour support provider uses this procedure. A provider that only carries out plans uses PRO-BSP-05 Supporting the Assessment and Development of Behaviour Support Plans Procedure.

Who acts:

  • The Service Manager logs the referral, sets the dates, allocates the people, prepares each lodgement and keeps the register.
  • The Clinical Lead triages the risk.
  • The Practitioner does every assessment, writes every plan and lodges it in the Commission's portal.
  • The Clinical Supervisor checks each report and each plan.
  • The Quality Manager and the Chief Executive check the register and receive anything late. The Quality Manager decides whether an incident is reportable and notifies the Commission.

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. A sole Practitioner holds the Service Manager, Quality Manager and Chief Executive roles, except that the decision whether an incident is reportable is made by the outside Clinical Supervisor with them. The Clinical Supervisor is always someone outside, is the Clinical Lead for this procedure, and does the Service Manager's checks on the sole Practitioner's own work. Where a step says to tell another role, a sole Practitioner writes it on the plan row and tells the Clinical Supervisor.

Terms in this procedure:

  • Practitioner: an NDIS behaviour support practitioner, a person the Commissioner considers suitable to assess behaviour and write plans (Behaviour Support Rules, section 5).
  • plan: a behaviour support plan, interim or comprehensive.
  • assessment report: the written record of the assessment, on FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template.
  • cover sheet: the record of how a plan was checked, shared and lodged, on FRM-BSP-02 Behaviour Support Plan Cover Sheet and Lodgement Record.
  • plan row: one line of REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register for one plan version.
  • implementing provider: a provider that carries out the strategies in a plan.
  • regulated restrictive practice: seclusion, chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, physical restraint or environmental restraint (Behaviour Support Rules, section 6).
  • engagement date: the date we agree in writing to develop the plan, or the date a regulated restrictive practice was first used, whichever is earlier (POL-SBS-03 ground rule 7). Where that use was before the referral reached us, the date the referral reached us. A later date named in a service agreement never moves it.
  • in force: a plan is in force from the date the Practitioner finalises and signs it.

3Before you start

  • You are a Practitioner the Commissioner considers suitable, or you are supporting one.
  • You can open REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register.
  • You have FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template and FRM-BSP-02 Behaviour Support Plan Cover Sheet and Lodgement Record, on paper or in the system.
  • You have the participant's communication preferences: FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form.
  • You know where FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form is kept.
  • You know your Clinical Supervisor's name and how to reach them.
  • You know the state or territory where the participant lives. Its law decides who can consent and which practices need authorisation.

4Watch out

  • If anyone is in danger, call 000 first. Tell the Service Manager after. A delay can cost a life.
  • Only a suitable Practitioner may assess or write. Anyone else doing it breaks a condition of our registration (Behaviour Support Rules, sections 17 and 18).
  • No consent, no assessment. Gathering information without valid consent breaches the participant's privacy and their right to decide.
  • Look for pain and illness first. A plan built on the wrong cause leaves the participant in pain and does not work.
  • The clocks start at engagement. Where a regulated restrictive practice led to our engagement, missing the 1 month or the 6 month limit breaks a condition of registration (Behaviour Support Rules, section 19).
  • A restrictive practice never enters through the back door. One that reaches a plan without consultation, notice and authorisation can be used on the participant unlawfully.
  • Lodge whether or not the practice is authorised. The Rules ask for the plan either way (Behaviour Support Rules, section 24(2)).
  • A plan nobody accepted may not be followed. Workers who have not seen it may respond in unsafe or uneven ways.

Decision table 1: Which plan do we write, and by when?

IfThenTime limit and source
A regulated restrictive practice was used, and we were engaged because of that useInterim plan first, under PRO-SBS-06 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support). Then a comprehensive plan. Both include the practice and go through PRO-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support)Interim: 1 month after the engagement date (statutory: Behaviour Support Rules, s 19(2)(a)). Comprehensive: 6 months after it (statutory: s 19(2)(b)). Our target for the comprehensive plan is 84 days
There is an immediate risk of harm to the participant or others, but no regulated restrictive practice has been usedInterim plan under PRO-SBS-06, written alongside the assessmentThe time PRO-SBS-06 sets. Comprehensive plan within 84 days of the engagement date (our standard)
A regulated restrictive practice is likely to be used soon but has not been usedInterim plan under PRO-SBS-06. Start PRO-SBS-02 before the practice is written into any planInterim plan within 1 month of the engagement date (our standard). Comprehensive plan within 84 days (our standard)
There is no immediate risk and no restrictive practiceAssessment, then a comprehensive planAssessment report within 49 days and plan within 84 days of the engagement date (our standard)

If a regulated restrictive practice is being used outside the plan, or the plan has lapsed, row 1 appliesReviewed plan lodged within 5 business days of our review (our standard). Comprehensive plan within 84 days of the engagement date (our standard). Section 19 is not triggered by a takeover of a lodged plan that is in force (NDIS Commission position statement, February 2026; legal reviewer to confirm)
A review or an event means the plan must changeA new version. Revisit the assessment first if the function may have changed. Repeat the plan stepsStart within 5 business days (our standard). Lodge the new version within 5 business days of finalising it if it contains a regulated restrictive practice (our standard)

The step limits for a comprehensive plan add up to about 77 calendar days: the report by day 49, then the check (3 business days), the findings and the draft together (5 business days), sending (1 business day), the providers' answers (5 business days), the final check (5 business days) and finalising (1 business day). That sits inside the 84-day target with a week in hand. Where a regulated restrictive practice led to our engagement, the 6-month limit in section 19(2)(b) is the law and the 84 days is our target inside it.

Decision table 2: Who gives consent?

IfThen
The participant is a childA person with parental responsibility decides. Take the child's views into account and tell them what is happening in a way they understand. Ask to see any court order that changes who decides

The participant is a young person assessed as able to consent in their own rightThe law of [state or territory] decides whether a young person may consent to an assessment. Where it allows, the young person decides, with support; record the basis. Involve a person with parental responsibility as the young person agrees or as the law requires
The participant can decide with supportThe participant decides. Use their way of communicating, give them time and offer an independent advocate. Consult family and carers only if the participant agrees
A guardian or another decision maker has legal authority for this decisionThe decision maker decides, with the participant's views in front of them. Look at the document. Record the name, the source of the authority and the date you saw it. The authority covers only what the document says

The participant says no, or stops laterStop collecting information. Record what they said. See If it goes wrong
There is an urgent risk and consent cannot be obtained yetDo only the risk work in PRO-SBS-06. Do not start the assessment until consent is in place

The law of [state or territory] says who may consent for an adult and which practices need authorisation. Look it up before the first meeting.

7If it goes wrong

IfThen
The participant says no, or stopsStop collecting information and share nothing more. Record what they said. Offer an independent advocate and more time. Tell the Service Manager. Ask again after 10 business days, if they agree (our standard). If there is a risk of harm, keep the interim safety work in PRO-SBS-06 going without the assessment
Nobody has authority and the participant cannot decideStop. Tell the Service Manager the same day. The Service Manager asks the referrer and the participant's advocate who can decide, and records the answer. Do not accept a family member's word alone
The plan has no behaviour support funding, or no suitable Practitioner is freeThe Service Manager tells the participant and the referrer in writing the same day. The message says what they can do: ask their support coordinator or the NDIA to change the plan, or choose another provider. Do not start paid work. If the risk is urgent, tell the Chief Executive, who decides whether to start with an interim plan and records the decision
The Practitioner is absent or leavesThe Service Manager gives the work to another suitable Practitioner within 2 business days. The first Practitioner, or the Clinical Supervisor, hands over the file. Tell the participant and their support network. The due dates do not move
An implementing provider declines or does not answerRecord each attempt. Ask why, and offer a change that keeps the participant safe. After 2 attempts the Service Manager tells the participant, and decides with the Clinical Supervisor whether to finalise and how to keep the participant safe. Record the decision. A plan finalised without a provider's acceptance is marked "not accepted by [provider]" at FRM-BSP-02 Q12, and the notice to the Commissioner under PRO-SBS-04 Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure starts the same day
A source will not give informationRecord your request and the reply. Carry on. List the gap in the assessment report. Never treat missing data as no behaviour
A due date will be missedTell the Service Manager as soon as you know, and at least 7 days before the date. The Service Manager tells the Chief Executive the same day, then the participant and each implementing provider. Record the reason, the new date and what keeps the participant safe in REG-SBS-01 col BB. The law lets nobody extend a limit it sets. For advice, phone the NDIS Commission on 1800 035 544. Never backdate a record
Lodgement failsTry again the same day. Save the error and the time. Phone the Commission. Record what happened in REG-SBS-01 col AP. If the due date has passed, tell the Chief Executive the same day
The plan is out of date or no longer fitsStart step 29 at once. Until the new version is in force, nobody uses a practice the plan does not contain. If a regulated restrictive practice is used outside the plan, follow PRO-SBS-05 Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support)
The participant disagrees with the planWrite their view in their words. Offer an independent advocate. Tell them they can complain under PRO-FBK-01 Feedback and Complaints Management Procedure. If the disagreement is about a restrictive practice, PRO-SBS-02 sets what happens next
You are worried about a colleague or a managerTell the Clinical Supervisor. If it is about the Clinical Supervisor, tell the Service Manager, who uses the substitute (PRO-SBS-01 Decision table 4). If it is about the Service Manager, tell the Chief Executive. If it is about the Chief Executive, or about a sole Practitioner's own work, tell the Clinical Supervisor or phone the NDIS Commission on 1800 035 544. If you think a participant has been abused, neglected or restrained unlawfully, follow PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure and PRO-SGD-01 Violence, Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation and Discrimination Procedure the same day
The participant leaves us or changes providerFollow PRO-SUP-04 Transitions to or from a Provider Procedure. With consent, give the new provider the current plan and the assessment report. Mark the row ended. Never delete it
The Practitioner is no longer considered suitableStop all assessment and plan work at once and tell the Service Manager. The Service Manager gives the work to another suitable Practitioner within 2 business days. The Clinical Supervisor checks the work already done before anyone relies on it. The due dates do not move
The system is downUse paper copies of FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template and FRM-BSP-02 Behaviour Support Plan Cover Sheet and Lodgement Record. The Service Manager enters them within 2 business days of the system coming back

8Done means

  • The assessment report is complete, signed off by the Clinical Supervisor and gone through with the participant.
  • The plan is finalised and in force, on a permitted template that holds every item in the Commission's checklist, with the Practitioner's endorsement.
  • Each implementing provider was consulted, was sent the draft and has an answer on record.
  • The participant has their plan in a form they understand.
  • A plan with a regulated restrictive practice has been through PRO-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) and lodged with the Commissioner, and the confirmation is filed.
  • Handover has started under PRO-SBS-03 Supporting the Implementation of the Behaviour Support Plan Procedure.
  • These records now exist:
    • the assessment report, FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template
    • the cover sheet, FRM-BSP-02 Behaviour Support Plan Cover Sheet and Lodgement Record
    • the consent record, FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form
    • the consultation record, FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record, where a practice is involved
    • a complete row in REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register.

form.intro:
Use this cover sheet and lodgement record for every behaviour support plan we write, interim or comprehensive. It records who wrote the plan and which template it is on. It records who has seen it and who accepted it. It also records whether the plan went to the Commissioner and where it is filed.

This sheet is not the plan, and it is not a form the Commissioner has approved. The plan itself is written on the Commission's current template, our own approved template that holds every item in the Commission's plan checklist, or the template a state or territory authorising body requires (Behaviour Support Rules, section 23(1)). A plan that contains a regulated restrictive practice is lodged by the Practitioner in the Commission's portal with the attachments it requires. Check the Commission's website for the current checklist and template edition on the day you start. This library does not reproduce the Commission's template.

The Practitioner completes sections A to E, except that the Clinical Supervisor answers Q14, and the Practitioner answers Q18 after lodging. The Service Manager answers Q17 and Q19 and prepares the lodgement.

Have ready:

  • the assessment report (FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template) and the participant's consent record (FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form)
  • the restrictive practice consultation record (FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record), if the plan has a practice
  • the contact details of each implementing provider.

What happens next: the Service Manager copies the answers marked for REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register to the plan row within 2 business days. The sheet is filed with the plan.

"Behaviour Support Rules" here means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.
form.privacy:
We collect this information to show that the plan was written, checked, shared and lodged as the law and the participant's wishes require. It names the participant and the providers who carry out their plan.

The Practitioner, the Clinical Supervisor, the Service Manager and the Quality Manager read it. We give the plan to the NDIS Commissioner when it contains a regulated restrictive practice. We share the plan with other people only as the participant, or their decision maker, agreed at Q9.

The participant can see this sheet and ask us to correct it. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store and protect it.
form.after:
1. The Practitioner gives the draft plan and this sheet to the Clinical Supervisor (PRO-BSP-03 step 24). The Clinical Supervisor answers within 5 business days, or 2 business days for an interim plan.
  2. After finalising, the Practitioner gives the Service Manager the finished plan and this sheet the same day (PRO-BSP-03 step 25).
  3. For a plan with a regulated restrictive practice, the Practitioner lodges it within 5 business days of the date at Q15, with the Service Manager preparing the lodgement (PRO-BSP-03 step 27).
  4. The Service Manager updates REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register within 2 business days of each stage (PRO-BSP-03 step 30).
  5. The plan, this sheet and the Commission's confirmation are filed together.
  6. A sole Practitioner does the Service Manager's tasks themselves. Their outside Clinical Supervisor does the check.

form.intro:
Use this template to write the assessment report. It shows what we found out about the participant and why, and what we recommend for their plan.

The Practitioner completes Sections B to J, and nobody else signs the clinical content. Section A is completed by the Service Manager from the plan row in REG-SBS-01 (PRO-BSP-03 steps 1 to 5), and the Practitioner copies the plan number into the report. Workers, family members and managers give information and records. They do not write findings. Only a specialist behaviour support provider uses this template. An implementing provider does not write assessment reports; it supplies behaviour records (FRM-BSP-04 Behaviour Record) to the Practitioner.

Start the report on the day the referral is logged. Fill it in as the assessment goes. Finalise it within 49 days of the engagement date (our standard).

Have ready:

  • the referral and the service agreement
  • the participant's communication preferences (FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form) and their consent record (FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form)
  • earlier plans and assessments, and the data from each implementing provider.

What happens next: the Clinical Supervisor checks the report within 3 business days. The Practitioner goes through it with the participant within 5 business days of the check. The Service Manager copies the answers marked for REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register to the plan row within 2 business days.

"Behaviour Support Rules" here means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.
form.privacy:
We collect this information to understand the participant and why they behave as they do, so we can write a plan that helps them. It holds sensitive information about their health, history and behaviour.

The Practitioner, the Clinical Supervisor and the Service Manager read it. We ask for information only from the people and services the participant agreed to (Q12), except that the law requires us to consult the providers who may use a restrictive practice; we tell the participant first and share only what they need. We share the report only with the people they agreed to (Q13). We give a plan with a regulated restrictive practice, and this report with it, to the NDIS Commissioner, as the Behaviour Support Rules require.

The participant can see this report and ask us to correct it. They can ask us to stop at any time. FRM-INF-02 Request to Access or Correct Personal Information Form is the form to ask. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store and protect it.
form.after:
1. The Practitioner gives the finished report to the Clinical Supervisor the same day (PRO-BSP-03 step 15).
  2. The Clinical Supervisor checks it within 3 business days and signs the sign-off block (PRO-BSP-03 step 16).
  3. The Practitioner goes through it with the participant within 5 business days of the check (PRO-BSP-03 step 17).
  4. The Service Manager copies each answer marked for REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register to the plan row within 2 business days (PRO-BSP-03 step 30).
  5. The report is filed on the participant's file. We share it only as Q13 says.
  6. A sole Practitioner files the report and updates the register themselves. The outside Clinical Supervisor does the check.

register.proves:
This register is the one running record of every behaviour support plan [Provider name] writes. It has three sheets. On the plan sheet each row is one plan version. It shows when we were engaged and who wrote the plan. It shows what the participant agreed to and which implementing providers accepted the plan. It shows whether the plan reached the Commissioner on time and when it is next due for review. On the practice sheet each row is one regulated restrictive practice in one plan, keyed on the plan number in col A, and holds the answers FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record routes here, with every authorisation status the practice has held. On the incident review sheet each row is one review under FRM-SBS-06 Restrictive Practice Incident Review Record of an emergency or unauthorised use, keyed on the plan number in col A.

"Behaviour Support Rules" here means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

  • Indicators evidenced: s 40 (1) to s 40 (6). The register also holds the plan dates and records that s 39, s 41, s 42, s 43 and s 44 rely on. Those threads write to the columns marked with their indicators.
  • Legal basis: the Behaviour Support Rules. Sections 17 and 18 say who writes. Section 19 sets time limits. Section 20 says how plans are developed and section 21 what they contain. Sections 22 to 24 cover review, form and lodgement.
  • Retention: keep each row for 7 years from the day the plan is superseded or ends (our standard). We set it to match the 7 years in section 15(3) of the Behaviour Support Rules for records of the use of a regulated restrictive practice.
  • Other law can require longer, for example for records about a child. For a participant under 18, keep the row until they turn 25 or for 7 years, whichever is later (our standard pending state law). Check REG-INF-02 Records Retention and Disposal Register and the law of [state or territory] before any row is destroyed.

Columns H and I are worked out and never typed over. Columns AB, AC, AD and AW are filled only when col Z lists a regulated restrictive practice, and summarise the practice sheet. Columns AN to AP are filled only when col AM is yes. Columns AR to BA are filled from the forms named in the Filled from column. The practice sheet columns RP-A to RP-R are filled from FRM-SBS-02, one row per practice per plan. The incident review sheet columns IR-A to IR-O are filled from FRM-SBS-06, one row per review; col AZ summarises them.
register.entry:
1. The Service Manager opens the row and keeps it. A sole Practitioner does both. Open the row on the day we confirm the referral (our standard).
  2. Use one row for each plan version. A new version is a new row. Link it to the one it replaces in col D and col BD.
  3. The Practitioner gives each answer to the Service Manager within 1 business day of recording it on the form. The forms are FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template and FRM-BSP-02 Behaviour Support Plan Cover Sheet and Lodgement Record for the plan sheet, and FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record for the practice sheet. The Service Manager enters it within 2 business days of the stage (our standard).
  4. Columns that hold a list (col R, col Z, col AC, col AD, col AG, col AK, col AW and col BB, and practice sheet cols RP-P and RP-R) take a new dated line for each change. Never overwrite a line. An authorisation status is never typed over: every status the practice has held stays visible with its date.
  5. Never overwrite or delete an entry. A correction is a new version of the row, with the date, your name and the reason.
  6. Never type over a worked-out date. To change the engagement date in col F, record the reason and the name of the Clinical Lead who agreed.
  7. When systems are down, use the paper forms. The Service Manager enters them within 2 business days of the system coming back.
  8. When a row is about the work of the Service Manager or the Practitioner who keeps it, the Chief Executive holds it. When it is about the Chief Executive, the Clinical Supervisor holds it. In a sole practitioner provider the Practitioner keeps every row, and the outside Clinical Supervisor reviews them every month under How we review.
  9. The practice sheet is the second sheet of this register: one row per regulated restrictive practice per plan, keyed on the plan number in col A, with cols RP-A to RP-R. Open a practice row when col Z first lists or proposes the practice. The incident review sheet is the third sheet: one row per FRM-SBS-06 review, keyed on col A, with cols IR-A to IR-O; open a row when a review starts and summarise it in col AZ. A small provider can keep the other list columns on a further sheet in the same way; each line carries the plan number from col A.

A row is closed only when all of these are true:

  • the plan has been replaced by a later version that is in force, or the plan has ended, or the participant has left us, and col BD says which
  • every lodgement is done and recorded in col AO
  • every open line in col BB is done, or has moved to REG-QMS-01 Continuous Improvement Register with an owner and a due date
  • the Service Manager has checked the row and recorded the closing date.

• The Clinical Lead, the Clinical Supervisor, the Quality Manager and the Chief Executive can see every row.
  • The Service Manager can see every row and enters most of them.
  • A Practitioner can see the rows for the participants they work with.
  • A participant can ask to see their own rows. We remove other people's details first.
  • A row about the work of a person who keeps the register is visible only to the person who holds it under Entry rule 8.
  • An auditor and the Commission see rows only as the law allows or requires.
  • An implementing provider sees only the dates and parts of its own role, and only with the participant's consent.

Rows hold sensitive personal and health information. Keep the register in [system name], with a login for each person and a log of changes. Lock away any paper copy. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets the wider privacy rules.
register.rows: The rows are the data. They are kept in the workbook or system built to this specification, not in this document. The register has three sheets: the plan sheet (one row per plan version, cols A to BF), the practice sheet (one row per regulated restrictive practice per plan, cols RP-A to RP-R, keyed on col A) and the incident review sheet (one row per FRM-SBS-06 review, cols IR-A to IR-O, keyed on col A). Where a plan sheet cell would otherwise hold a list of practices or reviews, the second or third sheet holds the detail and the plan sheet cell summarises it. Every column name on the plan sheet is kept stable, because other documents cite the columns by name.
